newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Trading near top of price range.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Trading near top of price range.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries prices are trading at their highest levels in four months and analysts said further gains would have to be fueled by technical, rather than fundamental, factors.
The Treasury will sell $15.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $11.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
The calendar of fundamental economic news for the coming week is light. No data are due on Monday. Tuesday offers two privately gathered weekly reports on chain store sales.

Two reports on consumer psychology -- the Conference Board's June consumer confidence index and the University of Michigan's final June consumer sentiment index -- are due on Tuesday and Friday, respectively.

The first government report on the economy -- durable goods orders data for June -- does not come until Wednesday. And the final estimate of real Gross Domestic Product growth that the Commerce Department will release on Friday is a first-quarter statistic and thus of little interest to the market.

Thursday's weekly jobless claims report could prove more interesting. For one thing, it provides a snapshot of the labor market in June. And secondly, claims have been creeping higher of late, and a continuation of that trend might give credence to the notion that the labor market is cooling a bit.

"Fundamentally, the news that is coming out next week is not of great importance," said Ryan Johanson, manager of two Northstar fixed-income funds with assets totaling more than $200 million. "But no news is good news. People have money to put to work. Money managers have been reluctant buyers, but they have to put their money to work."
Ryan said the market could build on its recent gains.
"The September long bond contract is at 112-12 and it could print 113 next week," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 99-18/32 on Friday, its yield at 6.66 percent.
Mark Pittman, who helps manage $3.0 billion in fixed-income assets at Milwaukee, Wisc.-based Marshall Funds, said if the market goes higher in coming week, "it will be purely on technicals.
"Economically and fundamentally, the market will be hard to impress," he said.

"The only significant economic number is the May durable goods report," said Pittman, who looks for a 0.5 percent rise. "Everyone already knows that consumer confidence is high. everybody is employed. The financial markets are rising. Fundamentally, you can't make a case for the market to go higher, but the technical guys are still excited."
Pittman said in addition to the Treasury's auctions of two- and five-year notes, "a huge supply" of asset-backed issuance could pressure the market a little, especially at the short end.

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., argued that it would be difficult for the market to squeeze out further gains from these levels without evidence that the economy was slowing in the second half of the year.

"The spread between the two-year note yield and the Federal funds rate is about 50 basis points," he said. "That's very tight, tighter than what you'd be expecting if the Fed were to hold policy steady indefinitely. I have trouble envisioning how the market can improve from here."
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Monday.
